profile.address: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Third Street, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Roane County, East Tennessee, Tennessee
profile.reading: This is Oak Ridge National Laboratory computing facility in Roane County, Tennessee, part of the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility overseen by the Center for Computational Sciences since 1992. The laboratory is sponsored by the United States Department of Energy and administered by UT-Battelle, LLC, a partnership between the University of Tennessee and Battelle Memorial Institute formed in 2000. This facility has hosted a succession of flagship supercomputers: the Intel Paragon XP/S 150 in 1995, Jaguar from 2005 to 2009 reaching 2.3 petaflops, Titan in 2012 reaching 17.59 petaflops and ranked number 1 on the TOP500 list that November, Summit in 2018 benchmarked at 122.3 petaflops with 202,752 CPU cores and 27,648 Nvidia Tesla GPUs, and Frontier, which broke the exaflop barrier in May 2022 at 1.102 exaflops per second using 8,730,112 cores and ranked third on TOP500. As a Department of Energy national laboratory computing facility, this serves federally funded scientific research rather than commercial purposes, and its scale is described in supercomputer performance terms rather than commercial colocation metrics.

reading.body:
Frontier at Oak Ridge National Laboratory is a Department of Energy supercomputing facility, not a commercial data center campus. Its capacity is published only in supercomputer performance benchmarks rather than in power draw or colocation terms. Frontier reached 1.102 exaflops per second in May 2022 using 8.73 million cores, ranked third globally on the TOP500 list, and serves federally funded scientific research rather than commercial AI training or inference workloads.

The facility cannot be translated into commercial rack or accelerator density without power specifications that are not published. Oak Ridge has historically hosted successive flagship supercomputers, most recently Summit at 122.3 petaflops before Frontier. Whether Frontier's hardware and infrastructure can or will be repurposed for commercial AI workloads is not stated in available sources.

Tennessee's published data center capacity totals 12.13 MW across four facilities, though 24 sites are mapped in the state. Frontier's rank and contribution to this total cannot be determined because its power consumption is not published in commercial terms. This facility matters to AI compute capacity only if its exascale hardware and federal resources become available to commercial generative AI research, which the available record does not indicate.
